steps.stem: A small cart moves at 4 meters per second. How many kilometers does it travel in 25 minutes?
explanation: In one minute there are sixty seconds, so the cart covers 4×60=240 metres. Twenty-five minutes give twenty-five groups of 240 metres: 6,000 metres. A kilometre is one thousand metres, so that is six kilometres. We changed seconds to minutes before using the twenty-five-minute interval.

steps.stem: A drone climbs along a straight line at 390 kph. After 2 minutes, its horizontal displacement is 12 kilometers. How high above its starting level is it, in kilometers?
explanation: Two minutes is one thirtieth of an hour. At 390 kilometres per hour, the drone travels thirteen kilometres along its sloping path. Draw a right triangle: twelve is the horizontal side, the unknown height is the vertical side, and thirteen is the sloping side opposite the right angle.
By Pythagoras, the height squared is thirteen squared minus twelve squared: 169−144=25. The height is five kilometres. Thirteen is the length of the flight path, so it is not the requested height.

steps.stem: A shuttle travels from a station to a hotel at 72 kph and returns along the same route at 48 kph, without stopping. What is its average speed for the whole round trip?
explanation: The one-way distance is not given, and its size will cancel. Choose 144 kilometres because both speeds divide it neatly. At seventy-two kilometres per hour the outward trip takes two hours. At forty-eight it takes three hours. The total is 288 kilometres in five hours, giving 57.6 kilometres per hour.

Average speed means total distance divided by total elapsed time. It is the one steady speed that would cover the whole route in the same overall time. It does not usually mean adding the two listed speeds and dividing by two. Here the slower speed lasts three hours while the faster one lasts only two.

This also explains why the answer is below sixty, the midpoint of the two speeds. More time is spent at forty-eight, so that speed has more influence on the time-weighted average. The simple average of sixty would be correct for equal times at the two speeds, but these journeys have equal distances.

steps.stem: Noor and Eli start at the same time from opposite ends of a path and walk towards one another. Eli walks at 1.75 times Noor’s speed. What fraction of the path does Noor cover before they meet?
explanation: Noor’s and Eli’s speed ratio is 1:1.75. Multiply both entries by four to make whole-number units: 4:7. They start together and we stop measuring at the same meeting, so they walk for equal amounts of time. Their distances so have that same ratio, four to seven.

The full path consists of Noor’s four distance units plus Eli’s seven. That makes eleven in all. Noor covers four of those eleven, giving four elevenths. The denominator is eleven because the question asks for Noor’s share of the whole path, not Noor’s distance compared only with Eli’s distance.

Imagine dividing the path into eleven equal strips. Noor walks across four strips from one end while Eli walks across seven from the other. Both arrive at the same dividing point. The strips represent relative distances; we are not claiming they are one metre long. Any common strip length leads to the same fraction.

steps.stem: Two boats leave opposite ends of a canal at the same time. Boat B is 3.5 times as fast as boat A. By the time B has traveled the full length of the canal, what fraction of that length has A traveled?
explanation: The speed ratio A:B is 1:3.5, or 2:7. Over the same time, A covers two distance units while B covers seven. This time, B’s seven units alone represent the whole canal, because the question ends when B reaches the far end. A so covers two sevenths.

We do not add two and seven to make nine. That would describe their combined distances up to a meeting between them. Here the endpoint is B finishing its own full journey. Drawing the starting points is useful, but identifying when the clock stops is what tells us which distance is the whole.

steps.title: Motion — rules to know
steps.intro: Motion is a work problem where the work is distance.

tables.title: Units
head: Fact
Note
rows: work in ONE set of units

tables.title: Relative speed
head: Situation
Speed of the gap
rows: one "stands still"; the other gains one lap

tips: Average speed \(=\) total distance \(:\) total time — not the average of the speeds.
In a chase, the only distance that matters is the gap at the start.

steps.stem: Two walkers leave the same gate at the same time in opposite directions along a straight path. Their speeds are 5 and 7 kph. After how many minutes are they 800 meters apart?
explanation: Every hour, one walker adds five kilometres to one side of the gap and the other adds seven to the other side. Their separation so grows at twelve kilometres per hour. The requested separation is eight hundred metres, or 0.8 kilometres.

Time is distance divided by relative speed: \(\frac{0.8}{12}=\frac1{15}\) of an hour. One fifteenth of sixty minutes is four minutes. We add the speeds here because the walkers move away from each other in opposite directions.

steps.stem: At 08:00 a van leaves Pine for Lake at 60 kph. At 08:30 a car leaves Lake for Pine at 90 kph. The towns are 105 kilometers apart. When do they meet?
explanation: During the first half hour only the van moves. At sixty kilometres per hour it covers thirty kilometres. At 08:30, when the car starts, the remaining gap is 105−30=75 kilometres.

From then on they move towards each other, so the gap closes at 60+90=150 kilometres per hour. A seventy-five-kilometre gap takes half an hour to close at that rate. Half an hour after 08:30 is 09:00.

The relative-speed calculation begins when both are moving. Using the original 105-kilometre distance with the combined speed would incorrectly give the car credit for travelling before it actually left.

steps.stem: Mina walks from home at 3 kph. Twenty minutes later, Owen leaves the same home along the same route and catches Mina 40 minutes after Owen starts. What is Owen’s speed?
explanation: Mina’s twenty-minute head start is one third of an hour. At three kilometres per hour, she gets one kilometre ahead. Owen closes that gap in forty minutes, or two thirds of an hour. Closing one kilometre in two thirds of an hour requires a speed advantage of one and a half kilometres per hour.

That one and a half is the difference between their speeds. Mina is still walking while Owen catches up. Add Mina’s three to get Owen’s speed of four and a half kilometres per hour. Reporting only the speed difference would make Owen slower than Mina, so it could not describe a successful chase.

steps.stem: Vehicle A travels 9 kilometers in 12 minutes. Vehicle B travels 12 kilometers in 9 minutes. What is the difference between their speeds, in kph?
explanation: Twelve minutes fits into an hour five times, so A’s speed is five times nine, or forty-five kilometres per hour. For B, multiply twelve kilometres by sixty and divide by nine: 720 divided by nine is eighty kilometres per hour. The speed difference is 80−45=35.

For the final subtraction, bridge through a round number if helpful: eighty minus forty is forty, then subtract five more to get thirty-five. Or shift both numbers up by five, giving 85−50=35. Adding the same amount to both numbers preserves their difference.

steps.stem: A cable carriage normally travels along a 180-meter cable in 12 seconds at a constant speed. On one trip, it travels the first half at twice its normal speed and the second half at half its normal speed. How many seconds does the trip take?
explanation: At the normal speed, each half of the cable takes six seconds. For the first half, doubling the speed halves the time, so that part takes three seconds. For the second half, halving the speed doubles the time, so that part takes twelve seconds. The total is fifteen seconds.

Doubling and halving the speeds do not cancel. They apply to equal distances, not equal time intervals. The slower half adds six seconds compared with normal, while the faster half saves only three. The trip is so three seconds longer overall.

steps.stem: B is the midpoint of a straight route from A to C. One cyclist rides from A to C at 24 kph. Another takes 20 minutes from A to B, then rides from B to C at 18 kph. Their total journey times are equal. How many kilometers long is AC?
explanation: Call each half x kilometres, so the whole route is 2x. The first cyclist’s time is \(\frac{2x}{24}=\frac{x}{12}\) hours. The second takes one third of an hour for the first half and \(\frac{x}{18}\) hours for the second.

Equal journey times give \(\frac{x}{12}=\frac13+\frac{x}{18}\). Multiply by thirty-six to remove the denominators: 3x=12+2x, so x=12. That is one half of the route. The requested whole distance is 2x=24 kilometres.

Choosing x for a half avoids repeatedly writing half of a whole-distance variable. Either choice works, but defining the smaller repeated piece makes the equation easier to read. The final doubling matters because x is not the quantity asked for.

steps.stem: A train covers a 1,350-kilometer route in 9 hours. A replacement train travels 80% faster. How many hours does the replacement take on the same route?
explanation: Eighty percent faster means the new speed is 180% of the old speed, a multiplier of 1.8. Because the distance stays the same, divide the old time by 1.8. Nine divided by 1.8 is five hours. Multiplying both parts of that division by ten gives ninety divided by eighteen, which may be easier to calculate.

An eighty-percent increase in speed does not mean an eighty-percent decrease in time. Speed and time multiply to the fixed distance, so their multipliers must multiply to one. The time multiplier here is five ninths.

steps.stem: Two cyclists start together from the same point of a circular track, riding in the same direction. The track is 600 meters long. Their speeds are 30 and 24 kph. How many minutes pass between consecutive meetings?
explanation: At the start the cyclists are together. The faster cyclist then moves ahead. Their next meeting occurs when the faster cyclist has gained exactly one complete lap on the slower one. It does not happen merely when the faster cyclist returns to the starting line, because the slower cyclist has moved too.

The speed advantage is thirty minus twenty-four, or six kilometres per hour. That is the rate at which the faster cyclist gains distance. One track lap is six hundred metres, or 0.6 kilometres. Gaining 0.6 kilometres at six kilometres per hour takes one tenth of an hour: six minutes.

We can picture the slower cyclist as standing still while the faster one moves at the relative speed of six kilometres per hour. This does not describe either person’s actual motion on the ground; it describes how their positions change compared with one another. In that relative picture, one complete lap returns the faster rider to the slower rider.

The same reasoning applies after every meeting. At any meeting they are alongside one another again, and the faster rider must gain one more full lap before the next one. With constant speeds the interval repeats every six minutes. The phrase consecutive meetings means there is no other meeting between the pair we are considering.

steps.stem: A cyclist completes one lap every 2 minutes at speed A and three laps every 8 minutes at speed B. She cycles for 24 minutes at each speed. How many laps does she complete?
explanation: At A, twenty-four minutes contains twelve two-minute laps. At B, it contains three eight-minute blocks, each worth three laps, giving nine. Total: twelve plus nine is twenty-one.

steps.stem: A ferry travels d kilometers in t hours. At three times that speed, how many kilometers does it travel in 2t hours?
explanation: Tripling speed triples the distance covered in the same time. Doubling the time doubles it again. The combined distance factor is 3×2=6, so the new distance is 6d.

steps.stem: A robot travels for x hours at 2x kph, then for y hours at 3y kph. What is its total distance?
explanation: The first stage covers x×2x, or \(2x^2\). The second covers y×3y, or \(3y^2\). Add the distances to get \(2x^2+3y^2\).

steps.stem: A coach travels from A to B at 64 kph for 3 hours. The route from B to C is 48 km longer. How long does B to C take at 80 kph?
explanation: A to B is 64×3=192 km. Add 48 to get 240 km for B to C. At eighty kilometres per hour, that takes 240:80=3 hours.

steps.stem: A taxi travels from A to B at 72 kph in 1 hour 20 minutes. It returns along the same route at 48 kph. How long does the return take?
explanation: The return speed is two thirds of the outward speed, so return time is one and a half times as long. One and a half times eighty minutes is 120 minutes, or two hours.

steps.stem: A delivery takes 4 hours at a constant speed. How long would the same trip take at 1.6 times that speed?
explanation: For a fixed distance, speed and time change in opposite proportions. Divide four hours by 1.6 to get 2.5 hours, which is two hours thirty minutes.

steps.stem: A fast cyclist chases a slower cyclist along a straight road. The slow cyclist rides at 12 kph, and the fast cyclist at 30. The initial gap is 9 km. How long until the fast cyclist catches up?
explanation: The gap shrinks at 30−12=18 kilometres per hour. Closing nine kilometres takes half an hour, or thirty minutes.

steps.stem: A walker leaves at 08:00, walks at 4 kph, and arrives at 11:00. Another walker covers the same route at 6 kph. When should the second walker leave to arrive at 11:00?
explanation: The route is 4×3=12 km. At six kilometres per hour it takes two hours. Two hours before 11:00 is 09:00.

steps.stem: A van travels 360 km. It covers the first 120 km at 60 kph, then one quarter of the remaining distance at 120, and the rest at 30. How many hours does the whole trip take?
explanation: After 120 km, 240 remain. One quarter of that is sixty, leaving 180 for the final stage. The times are 120:60=2, 60:120=0.5, and 180:30=6 hours. Total: 8.5 hours.

steps.stem: Two runners leave the same point on a circular track in opposite directions. One runs five times as fast as the other. At their first meeting, what central angle corresponds to the arc traveled by the slower runner?
explanation: At their first meeting, their distances add to one full circumference. The distances are in the same 5:1 ratio as their speeds. The slower runner covers one sixth of the circle, corresponding to 360°:6=60°.

steps.stem: Two buses travel the same 180-km route, starting together. Bus A is 15 kph faster than Bus B. How much earlier does A arrive?
choices: It cannot be determined from the information given.
explanation: At speeds 45 and 30, the trip times are four and six hours, a two-hour gap. At speeds 90 and 75, the times are two and 2.4 hours, a twenty-four-minute gap. The same speed difference can produce different arrival gaps.

steps.stem: A swimmer covers 1.8 km each morning and 2.4 km each evening. Her morning speed is 60 meters per minute; her evening speed is half as great. How many minutes does she swim in a day?
explanation: The morning distance is 1,800 m, taking 1,800:60=30 minutes. Evening speed is thirty metres per minute, so 2,400 m takes eighty minutes. Together that is 110 minutes.

steps.stem: A signal travels through a cable at \(200{,}000{,}000\) meters per second. How far does it travel in \(3\times10^{-9}\) seconds?
explanation: The speed is \(2\times10^8\). Multiply by \(3\times10^{-9}\) to get \(6\times10^{-1}=0.6\) metre.

steps.stem: Two cyclists start together and ride in the same direction on a 3-km circular track. Their speeds are 15 and 9 kph. After how many minutes does the faster rider first lap the slower one?
explanation: Lapping means gaining three kilometres. The gain rate is 15−9=6 kilometres per hour. Three kilometres at that rate take half an hour, or thirty minutes.

steps.stem: Two vans leave together on the same road. One travels at 90 kph, the other at 60. After 180 km, the faster van stops for 1.5 hours. How many hours after departure does the slower van first catch it?
explanation: The faster van reaches 180 km after two hours. The slower van has covered 120 km, leaving a sixty-kilometre gap. It needs one more hour to reach the stopped van, which is still within the 1.5-hour stop. Catch-up occurs after three hours.

steps.stem: A road from A to B is 140 km long. At 08:00 a car leaves A toward B. At 09:00 another car leaves B toward A at the same speed. They meet 30 km from B. What is their common speed?
explanation: The first car covers 110 km and the second 30 km. Their speeds are equal, so the extra eighty kilometres travelled by the first car comes entirely from its one-hour head start. The speed is eighty kilometres per hour.

steps.stem: A car travels a total distance D in 4 hours. It covers half the distance at speed v and half at speed 3v. How long would the whole distance take at speed v?
explanation: Let the whole route at speed v take T hours. The slow half takes \(\frac T2\) and the fast half takes \(\frac T6\). Together \(\frac{2T}{3}=4\), giving T=6.

steps.stem: A robot makes 40 equal jumps per minute and moves at 18 kph. How long is each jump?
explanation: Eighteen kilometres per hour is 18,000:60=300 metres per minute. Forty jumps cover those 300 metres, so each jump is 300:40=7.5 metres.

steps.stem: Two runners start together on a 500-meter circular track and run in opposite directions at the same speed. Each runs exactly 3,750 meters. How many times do they meet after the start, including the finish if they meet then?
explanation: Each meeting occurs whenever their combined distance grows by one circumference. Together they cover 7,500 m. Dividing by 500 gives fifteen meetings after the initial one. The last occurs exactly at the finish and is included.

steps.stem: At 10:00, a walker leaves A toward B at 6 kph. A second walker leaves B later at 9 kph. They meet halfway between A and B at 10:45. How many minutes later did the second walker start?
explanation: The first walker travels for forty-five minutes, covering 4.5 km. The second covers the same distance at nine kilometres per hour, taking thirty minutes. To arrive at 10:45, the second leaves at 10:15: fifteen minutes later.

steps.stem: A cyclist rides 24 km at 12 kph and returns along the same route at 8. What is the average speed for the whole trip?
explanation: The outward trip takes two hours and the return three. Total distance is forty-eight kilometres in five hours, so average speed is 48:5=9.6 kilometres per hour.

steps.stem: Two trains start 420 km apart and move toward each other at 80 and 60 kph. After how many hours do they meet?
explanation: Each hour, the gap falls by 80+60=140 km. A 420-km gap so closes in three hours.

steps.stem: A runner travels at 3 meters per second. How many kilometers does she cover in 25 minutes?
explanation: Twenty-five minutes is 1,500 seconds. At three metres per second, the distance is 4,500 metres, or 4.5 kilometres.

steps.stem: A boat moves at 15 kph in still water. The current is 3 kph. How long does a 72-km downstream trip take?
explanation: Downstream, the current adds to the boat’s still-water speed, so the ground speed is eighteen kilometres per hour. Seventy-two kilometres take four hours.

steps.stem: A train 180 meters long passes a stationary post in 12 seconds at constant speed. How long does it take to pass completely through a 270-meter tunnel?
explanation: Passing the post gives speed 180:12=15 metres per second. To clear the tunnel, the train’s front travels the tunnel length plus the train length: 450 metres. Time is 450:15=30 seconds.

steps.stem: A cyclist leaves at 07:00 at 16 kph. Another leaves the same place at 07:30 at 24. At what time does the second cyclist catch the first?
explanation: The first cyclist gets eight kilometres ahead in half an hour. The second closes that gap at 24−16=8 kilometres per hour, taking one hour after 07:30. The catch is at 08:30.

steps.stem: A driver covers the first half of a journey in 2 hours and the second half in 3 hours. If the total distance is 240 km, how much faster is the first-half speed?
explanation: Each half is 120 km. The first speed is 120:2=60, and the second is 120:3=40 kilometres per hour. Their difference is twenty.
